column2: The Mantrinatha sang on the great wheel-chariot, the finest of chariots; its seven tiers have been told — hear now of the goddesses there.
On the Geyachakra chariot, dwelling on the central seat of its tiers, is the one called Sangitayogini, most beloved of the Goddess.
That is the first tier, the dwelling of the Mantrini. Then in the second tier of the Geyachakra, the finest of chariots,
are Rati, Priti and Manoja, holding lute and bow, dark as the tamala tree, able to uproot the Danavas.
Established in the third tier are the deities of the arrows of Love: Dravini, Shoshini, Bandhini, Mohini
and Unmadini — these five hold blazing bows. Below them in that tier dwell the mighty ones:
Kamaraja, Kandarpa, Manmatha, Makaradhvaja and Manobhava the fifth — these bewitch the three worlds.
Their foreheads bright with musk marks and adorned with pearls, their bodies wholly covered in armour, radiant like palasha blossoms —
these are declared the five Kamas, intent on slaying Bhandasura. In the fourth tier of the king of chariots, the Geyachakra, dwell
the goddesses led by Brahmi named before, with Chandika the supreme eighth. Below them in that tier are Lakshmi and Sarasvati,
and the Shaktis Rati, Priti, Kirti, Shanti, Pushti and Tushti; these, their eyes red with anger, are ready to slay the mighty Daitya.
They are declared to be maidens bearing lances and discuses, O pot-born one. In the fifth tier are sixteen others beginning with Vama,
who sang for the king of chariots; hear their names from me: Vama, Jyeshtha, Raudri, Shanti, Shraddha, Sarasvati,
Shri, Bhushakti, Lakshmi, Srishti, Mohini, Pramathini, Ashvasini, Vichi,
Vidyunmalini, Surananda and Nagabuddhika. These, like rubies, are eager to shake the world,
bearing great armour at every step; others, covered in diamond mail and bright with loud laughter, hold diamond staffs, shataghnis and bhushundis.
Then in the sixth tier of the king of song-chariots are the Bhairavas beginning with Asitanga, fearsome with weapons,
bearing tridents and drinking vessels, dark in lustre: Asitanga, Ruru, Chanda, Krodha, Unmatta Bhairava,
Kapali, Bhishana and Samhara — the eight Bhairavas. Then in the seventh tier of the king of song-chariots are
Matangi, Siddhalakshmi, Mahamatangika and the great Siddhalakshmi, red in hue, bearing bows and arrows.
Below that same tier are Ganapa and Kshetrapa, Durgamba and Batuka, all holding weapons in their hands.
Below that same tier are also Lakshmi and Sarasvati, and the treasures Shankha and Padma, all holding weapons.
Enraged against Bhanda of fierce valour, enemy of the worlds, the ten guardians of the circle of directions, from Shakra to Vishnu,
in the form of Shaktis, have taken their place below in that tier, bearing thunderbolt, spear, the staff of death, sword, noose and banner,
mace, trident, the darbha missile and the vajra; ever filled with devotion, they serve the Mantrinatha.
To slay the Bhandasuras, hard to overcome, thorns of the universe, eager for Lalita's command by resorting to the Mantrinatha,
the guardians of the directions took shelter near the Geyachakra chariot. The Mantrini is made the gateway for all the gods;
a request to the great Goddess made through her grants success in one's aims. A request to the Queen is made through the chief minister,
just as servants obtain their reward that way. Otherwise how could these, however blazing in might, have the power
to approach the Goddess, whose power is unassailable? For she, the science of music, is most beloved of the Goddess.
The Goddess never oversteps what she says in the accomplishment of tasks. In the empire of the Goddess's Shaktis, the Mantrini is able
to do, to undo and to do otherwise all actions. Therefore all the guardians of the directions, desiring the Goddess's victory, serve her who is the chief.
Thus the names of the goddesses stationed in the tiers of Shri Lalita's Chakraraja, the finest of chariots, have been fully told.
Her divine weapons for the destruction of Bhandasura have also been described, and the goddesses of the tiers of the Geyachakra celebrated.
Those men who listen to these names of all the goddesses become free of all sins and victorious.
Shakini and Dakini, and the one whose form is their unity, Hakini the seventh — these have the might of fierce arms,
as if drinking up beings, as if drinking up the earth, drinking the skin, blood, flesh, fat and bones of their enemies,
the marrow and the semen, with gaping mouths, filling the ten directions with harsh lion-roars.
They are called the Dhatunathas, givers of the eight perfections beginning with minuteness, skilled in bewitching, killing, paralysing and striking,
in devouring the wicked Daityas and cutting them down to the root; they destroy all the misfortunes of those rich in devotion.
They are called the Dhatunathas, dwelling in all the bodily elements. They could drink up all seven oceans, whose garlands of waves kiss the sky,
in half a moment, having accomplished many bold deeds; their teeth like cart-wheels, their eyes terrifying.
They are equal to devouring those who betray their own mistress, who break their own vows, who are hostile to the Veda, enemies of heroes,
and the wicked Daityas who obstruct sacrifices; and they always serve Potrini, the Dandanayika.
Beside that same tier, in a second divine chamber, dwell the two famous goddesses Krodhini and Stambhini,
fanning with chowries, their creeper-like arms with swaying bracelets, exultant from drinking the red wine of the armies of the gods' enemies,
their eyes ever rolling and their faces ever laughing. Then, on that king of chariots, the Kirichakra,
dwelling on its two sides, is a pair of excellent weapons, the plough and the pestle, which have taken the form of deities,
bearing their own weapon-forms in place of their crowns; they are remembered by the wise as devourers of the world.
With this pair of weapons the Dandanayika of Lalita will cut down in battle the Danava named Vishanga.
At the front edge of that tier of the Dandanatha is a very terrible lion, resounding in the sky with its roars,
deafening the quarters with the gnashing of its fangs, famed as Chandochchanda, four-handed and three-eyed,
bearing spear, sword and the noose of the dead, of blazing form, ever serving the Goddess, gazing constantly at Potrini.
In the sixth tier of the Kirichakra, king of chariots, dwell the eight goddesses beginning with Vartali, renowned in the eight directions,
their cries like the terrible crash of eight mountains falling, adorned with eight shining serpents, of undiminished strength and splendour,
who have offered crores of Danavas into the heat of their mighty arms; these goddesses serve Lalita's Dandanatha day and night.
Hear their famous names, O pot-born one: Vartali, Varahi, the boar-faced one, the supreme,
Andhini, Rodhini, Jrimbhini, Mohini and Stambhini — able to agitate, paralyse and drive away enemies.
On the left side of their tier always stands the mount of the Dandanatha, a buffalo of dusky form,
half a krosha long in its two horns and a krosha in body, its body covered with hair harsh as swords,
terrifying with its fierce tail like the staff of death, like a mountain of blue collyrium, its brow terrible, lofty and angry,
its shoulders massive as the best of great blue mountains, making the ocean tremble with the blast of its hot breath,
as if mocking the buffalo of Death with its rumbling roar, scattering the Pushkalavarta clouds with its hooves.
Below that same tier, dwelling in various places, are Indra and the other deities of the eight directions in many divisions,
who have come to request success in their task from Lalita: Indra and the Apsarases, sixty-four crores of them,
the Siddhas, Agni, the Sadhyas, the Vishvedevas and others, Vishvakarman, Maya and the Mothers exalted in strength,
the Rudras and their attendants, the Rudras and the Pishachas, the lord of the Rakshasas and many Rakshasas,
the Mitras, and the Gandharvas ever skilled in song, the famous ones led by Vishvavasu,
and other hosts of beings, Varuna, Vasava and others, the Vidyadharas, Kinnaras and the lord of the winds,
Chitraratha and the chariot-makers, Tumburu, Narada, the Yaksha, and Soma the lord of Yakshas,
and with the gods the Lord Govinda, husband of Kamala, and Ishana, devourer of the circle of the world, fearsome with his trident,
Brahma, and the two sons of the Ashvini skilled in medicine, the Lord Dhanvantari, and the other leaders of the Ganas,
whose temples drip with ichor that satisfies the bees; Ananta, Vasuki, Takshaka, Karkotaka and Padma,
Mahapadma, Shankhapala, Gulika and Subala — these lords of serpents, surrounded by crores of serpents.
Many deities of this kind keep watch there, their dwellings made all around, beginning from the eastern direction.
On that same chariot, the deities of the winds and directions, wheel-shaped, abide as its presiding deities.
Jrimbhini, Stambhini and Mohini — these three. At the edge of that same tier of the shining Kirichakra,
bearing skull and mace, hair standing on end, of huge body, dark as the mud of the netherworld,
who split the circle of the cosmic egg with the great thunderbolt of his laughter, shattering the cavern of heaven and earth with the sound of his drum,
holding in his hand a serpent-noose joined with the hissing Tripura — the Kshetrapala always shines there, serving the queen of boars.
Near him stands her lion mount, on which she set forth desiring the slaughter of Bhandasura.
The marks of the lion that carries the Goddess were told earlier. Below that same tier, radiant like the Dandanatha,
adorned with all the ornaments and weapons like those of Dandini, are the boar-faced Shamyas, their locks crowned with the crescent moon,
whirling plough and pestle in their hands again and again; with overflowing streams of blood of those hostile to Lalita, to Shyama and to their mistress
they fill their skull-bowls; adorned with garlands of mantras, against those who harm their devotees,
they wear on their breasts garlands of the heads of those who disturb their assembly, dripping with unbroken streams of blood.
A thousand deities are declared to serve the queen of boars.
The names of all these attendants of Dandini, O pot-born one, will be told in the chapter of the thousand names, not again now.
Then, near those boar-faced deities, stands Dandini's mount, the black buck, in readiness,
its horns a quarter of a krosha long, its face an eighth, its feet a krosha in measure, its tail always raised,
white on its belly, with a mighty snort mocking the prowess of the deer that carries the Wind.
In the region of that same tier stands the excellent mount of the Kirichakra, king of chariots; and in that same tier
abides the ocean of wine in the form of a deity, holding in her hand a lump of flesh red as a ruby mountain,
her eyes rolling, garlanded with golden lotuses, embraced by the Shakti of intoxication who holds a red lotus.
Whenever the Daitya Bhanda engages in battle and the Shaktis, sweating from the fighting, become thirsty,
then the ocean of wine, casting itself forth in many ways, will swiftly remove the weariness of the goddesses in battle.
That too will be a great wonder, without doubt; then you will hear it gladly told by me in the account of the battle.
Below that same tier, in the eight directions below and above, dwell the ten remembered as beginning with Hetuka,
great, foremost Bhairavas, famed for vast valour, who with blazing splendour light up the suns in heaven,
devourers of the universe at the end of the kalpa at Dandini's command, of exceedingly fierce nature, biting their lips with their teeth,
who have split the great circles of clouds with the points of their tridents: Hetuka, Tripurari, the third Agnibhairava,
Yamajihva and Ekapada, Kala and Karalaka, Bhimarupa, Hatakesha and the one named Achala.
These ten are famous, each accompanied by ten crores of warriors; they stand at the boundary of that tier of the Kirichakra.
Thus the deities of the Dandanatha's Kirichakra, from Jrimbhini to Achalendra, purifiers of the three worlds, have been told.
By the hosts of deities there, many Danavas will be slain in that battle and rains of blood will be drunk.
Thus protected in many ways by the hosts of deities in its tiers, the Kirichakra, jewel of chariots of the Dandanetri, moved forward.
Where the Chakraraja chariot was, there was the finest Geya chariot; and where the Geya chariot was, there was the finest Kirichakra chariot.
These three chariots, like the three worlds in motion, then moved auspiciously amid thousands of armies of Shaktis.
It was like a gathering of Meru, Mandara and Vindhya. A great din arose in the circle of the Shakti army; the whole earth shook, split by the noise of those wheels.
Lalita's chariot is called the Chakraraja; six charioteers are declared for that lord of chariots, skilled in handling the mighty reins.
Where the Geya chariot is, there is the finest Kirichakra chariot. First is the Goddess herself, then Tripurabhairavi,
Samharabhairava, another beloved of the Raktayoginis, Sarasa the fifth, and Chamunda likewise.
These deities are remembered as the charioteers there. The charioteer of the Geyachakra, king of chariots, is Hasantika;
Stambhini is remembered as the charioteer of the Kirichakra, king of chariots. Lalita's foremost chariot is ten yojanas high;
the excellent Gitachakra chariot is seven yojanas high; the Kirichakra chariot is six yojanas high, O sage.
A great pearl umbrella ten yojanas wide is found only on the chariot of the Queen Lalita and nowhere else.
That alone is declared the emblem of the empire of the Shaktis; an ordinary umbrella is found on the other two.
Then Lalita the Queen, great mistress of all Shaktis, the supreme Goddess, having ascended to the rank of great empire,
set forth, desiring to accomplish the destruction of the Daitya Bhanda. All the directions resounded and the earth trembled;
all beings were stirred at Lalita's departure. The drums of the gods sounded and showers of flowers fell.
The Gandharvas led by Vishvavasu, singers of the gods, Tumburu and Narada, and Sarasvati herself,
reciting verses of victory and blessing in skilful songs, faces blooming with joy, adorned with bristling hair, praised Lalita, the Queen, crying again and again "Victory, victory!"
Full of joy, intoxicated, dancing at every step; the Seven Sages led by Vasishtha, with mantras in the form of Rig, Yajus and Saman
and in the form of Atharvan, increasing her glory of victory as oblations increase the exceedingly purifying flame of a great fire —
those excellent ones increased it with their great blessings. Praised by them, Lalita, shining on her excellent chariot,
went to conquer Bhandasura with her mighty soldiers.

Then this would be like splitting a stone by breaking off a sprig; to go out and kill her would be made a matter of ridicule.
brahmandpuran:133:38	Is this not a mockery? Is it not shameful? She would be afraid even of the vanguard soldiers of our army.
brahmandpuran:133:39	The heaven-dwellers led by Shakra have become cowards, and Brahma and the others are dejected in body by the weapons of my army.
brahmandpuran:133:40	What to say of Vishnu? Even Maheshvara is terrified. What talk of others here? The guardians of the directions have fled.
brahmandpuran:133:41	With our sharp, invisible arrows that fell upon their limbs, the arrogant gods everywhere have had their armour pierced.
brahmandpuran:133:42	Against us, who possess such mighty and valiant arms, some woman now rushes forward for victory!
brahmandpuran:133:43	Though she is a woman, she should never be despised; an enemy, however small, should not be despised by the self-aware seeking victory.
brahmandpuran:133:44	Therefore servants should be sent to drive her off; that intoxicated woman should be dragged here by the hair.
brahmandpuran:133:45	O lord, that wicked one will long serve as a maidservant to the doe-eyed women of your inner apartments.
brahmandpuran:133:46	From any single warrior of our army, the three worlds with all that moves and does not move are terrified.
But the lord's mind is the final authority, said the Danava; having reported thus, he increased the anger of the Daitya Bhanda.
But Vishanga, of great strength, discerning and wise, said this to his elder brother, the arrogant great Daitya:

O lord, subduer of foes, you know every matter; nothing need be told to you who walk the path of policy.
brahmandpuran:133:50	Everything should be done after reflection; reflection is the highest recourse. If action is taken without reflection, it cuts one off at the root.
brahmandpuran:133:51	Spies should be sent with care into the enemy's camp; one who desires victory should learn their strength and weakness.
brahmandpuran:133:52	With spies for eyes, firm in wisdom, ever watchful in mind yet appearing unconcerned, keeping counsel secret among his ministers,
brahmandpuran:133:53	employing the six expedients, in a position honoured everywhere — such a king wins victory; the fool quickly perishes.
brahmandpuran:133:54	Any undertaking without reflection brings ruin; an act done after reflection especially brings victory.
brahmandpuran:133:55	Whether an animal, a woman or something small, kings should not despise their enemies; power may arise anywhere.
brahmandpuran:133:56	By a being born from a pillar, bearing a form half man and half beast, Hiranyakashipu, lord of all beings, was slain.
brahmandpuran:133:57	Long ago a woman named Chandika, unfolding her maya, slew Nishumbha, Shumbha and Mahisha in battle,
brahmandpuran:133:58	and in that connection many Daityas were destroyed by her. Therefore I say, let no contempt be shown even to a mere woman.
brahmandpuran:133:59	Power alone is everywhere the cause of victory and prosperity; we have no fear of those, male or female, who have become the vessels of power.
brahmandpuran:133:60	Power shines everywhere by the very nature of the world. So let the conduct of that ill-intentioned one be learned by you:
brahmandpuran:133:61	who she is, whence she arose, what her conduct and support are, what her strength and her allies — let that be considered, O lord.
Thus addressed by Vishanga, he said, "What need is there for reflection for the mighty? In our army are a hundred mighty commanders of akshauhinis,
able to drink up the oceans and burn up heaven. O you of sinful conduct, why do you needlessly fear a woman?
I have seen all this before through my spies. Some woman named Lalita has arisen in front of us.
She bears a name true to her nature, delicate in form like a flower; she has neither strength nor valour, nor any skill in battle.
She is thoughtless, devoted only to illusion; lacking strength herself, she has produced a crowd of women.
What can she do to you? She does not act thus. Or, by the reasoning you have stated, let her army be great —
by whom can Bhanda, whose greatness surpasses the three worlds, be conquered?
Even now the heavenly ones, fainting from the crushing force of my arms, are never able even to breathe.
Some in the depths of Patala, some in the waters of the ocean, some in the corners of the directions, some in the thickets of mountains,
they hide, greatly terrified, abandoning wives, sons and fortune; fallen from their offices, those beasts wander in disguise.
She does not know such prowess of my arms; being a weak woman, recently born, she is full of pride.
Foolish women do not know; imagining vain feats of daring, deluded about what should and should not be done, they run toward destruction.
Or if, placing her in front, the heavenly ones come — whether great serpents, Siddhas or Sadhyas proud in war,
Brahma, the lotus-naveled one, Rudra or the lord of the gods, or other lords of the quarters — I am able to crush them.
Or else the commanders of my armies, proud in battle, will crush the enemies like ripe cucumbers:
Kutilaksha, Kuranda, Karanka, Kalavashita, Vajradanta, Vajramukha, Vajraloman, Balahaka,
Suchimukha, Phalamukha, Vikata, Vikatanana, Karalaksha, Karkataka, Madana, Dirghajihvaka,
Humbaka, Halamulluncha, Karkasha, Kalkivahana, Pulkasa, Pundraketu, Chandabahu, Kukkura,
Jambukaksha, Jrimbhana, Tikshnashringa, Trikantaka, Chaturgupta, Chaturbahu, Chakaraksha, Chatuhshiras,
Vajraghosha, Urdhvakesha, Mahamaya, Mahahanu, Makhashatru, Makhaskandi, Simhaghosha, Shiralaka,
Andhaka, Sindhunetra, Kupaka, Kupalochana, Guhaksha, Gandagalla, Chandadharma, Yamantaka,
Laduna, Pattasena, Purajit, Purvamaraka, Svargashatru, Svargabala, the one called Durga, Svargakantaka,
Atimaya, Brihanmaya, Upamaya, Ulukajit, Purushena, Vishena, Kuntishena, Parushaka,
Malaka, Kashura, Mangala, Draghana, Kollata, Kujilashva, Dasera, Babhruvahana,
Drishtahasa, Drishtaketu, Parikshepta, Apakanchuka, Mahamaha, Mahadamshtra, Durgati, Svargamejaya,
Shatketu, Shadvasu, Shaddanta, Shatpriya, Duhshatha, Durvinita, Chhinnakarna, Mushaka,
Attahasi, Mahashi, Mahashirsha, Madotkata, Kumbhotkacha, Kumbhanasa, Kumbhagriva, Ghatodara,
Ashvamedhra, Mahanda, Kumbhanda, Putinasika, Putidanta, Putichakshus, Putyasya and Putimehana.
These heroes and others like them are equal to Hiranyakashipu; and my very mighty sons are equal to Hiranyaksha.
To each of them have been born more than a hundred heroic sons. My commanders, wild with pride, followed by my sons,
will destroy the arrogant, base immortals in battle. If a thousand excellent akshauhinis became enraged in battle, they would be reduced to ashes by them — alas, what then of a weak woman?
All her displays of illusion on the field of battle, and her great magical tricks — if they grew angry, her army would turn to ashes.
So let your mind not be troubled by needless fear." Having said this, Bhanda, lord of the Daityas, rose from the royal throne
and spoke to his own mighty general Kutilaksha: "Rise! Equip the whole army on every side.
Post forces at all the gates of Shunyaka round about. Take charge of the fortresses and set up a hundred catapults.
Wicked spells should be performed by the ministers and priests. Make ready the weapons; this war is at hand.
Send forward now some one of the generals, with a terrifying host of many forces.
Let him fall upon her in battle, conquer her, and drag that foolish woman, proud of the gods' support, by the hair."
Having spoken thus to the army commander Kutilaksha, lord of three thousand, of great strength, he himself went into the inner apartments.
Then the sounds of the marching drums of the approaching Goddess were heard by the Daitya lords, bringing fever to their ears.
The serpents, creeping out in masses, multiplied one above another; many serpents perished and others were born again.
At the moment one was destroyed, many others arose, because the wicked serpent-woman, their root, did not perish.
Hence when the serpents she created were destroyed, other serpents arose. And then the bodies of the Shakti armies, by the fire of the poison,
burning in pain, were thrown into confusion in the battle. While the circles of Shaktis were bewildered by the serpents as to what to do,
those five Danavas displayed many kinds of prowess. Karindri, mounted on a chariot yoked with a hundred donkeys,
crushed the Shakti army with a sharp-edged discus. Another, named Vajradanta, a commander of the Daitya Bhanda's army,
fought from a camel with blows of thunderbolt arrows. Then Vajramukha, mounting a great wheeled vehicle,
crushed the circle of Shaktis with streams of lances. Another mighty army commander named Vajradanta,
riding a chariot drawn by a pair of vultures, struck with arrows. Urged on by those wicked generals in the battle,
a hundred akshauhinis fell upon them in a single onslaught. And the evil serpent-woman, possessed of much sorcery,
moment by moment released crores of hooded serpents. Seeing the army thus disordered, filled with rage,
Nakuli, riding Garuda, swooped onto the battlefield — radiant like molten gold, born from Lalita's palate,
whose form is all speech, with teeth of diamond. There she sent forth her own force against the serpent-woman.
Garuda, his lofty shoulders occupied by her, scattering mountains with his wings, advanced into battle like Sumeru in motion.
Seeing the terrible serpents born of the serpent-woman's sorcery, Nakuli, her eyes red with anger, opened her mouth wide.
Then from the thirty-two crores of teeth of the goddess Nakuli were born thirty-two crores of golden mongooses.
Cutting to pieces the serpents of the serpent-woman here and there, destroying their poison by crushing with their fangs, the golden-brown poison-killers roamed the terrible battlefield.
Ears pricked up, every hair bristling with anger, the excited mongooses with gaping mouths bit the snakes.
For each illusory serpent one mongoose arose, and with the stroke of its sharp teeth cut its body to pieces.
Licking with their tongues the corners of their mouths reddened by blood streaming from the serpents' coils, the mongooses bounded about the battle.
The bodies of the serpents being bitten by the mongooses writhed most violently, their coils curling again and again.
The gems scattered from the hoods of the lifeless hooded serpents bitten by rows of mongooses glittered on the battlefield.
The gems issuing from the circles of hoods shattered by the mongooses' blows shone like flames of the fire of that great enmity.
When the illusory net of serpents was thus cut to pieces by the troops of mongooses, the serpent-woman became enraged.
Having fought a great battle with her, the queen of mongooses fixed the most dreadful Garuda missile on her arrow.
That Garuda missile, lighting up the quarters with its unrestrained flames, entered the serpent-woman's body and dried up her serpent sorcery.
With the destruction of her power of illusion, the serpent-woman perished; and at her destruction the five commanders became enraged.
The serpent-woman by whose strength those generals had despised all the gods was reduced to a mere memory by the valour of the mongooses.
Therefore, greatly enraged at the loss of their power, the commanders with one effort covered Nakuli with floods of weapons.
Alone, riding on Garuda against the five commanders, she, with swift hands, rained weapons in battle.
With pattishas, pestles and bhindipalas in thousands, and with teeth of diamond, she struck at their vital points.
Then the Daitya servants raised a terrible cry of woe, thrown into confusion by the fierce-biting mongooses.
Some, leaping from the sky with terrible shrieks, bit the enemy army together with their kin, blazing with anger.
Some bit at the ears, others at the nose, others on the head; some came from behind and bit, disrupting their actions.
Distressed, their armour cut, their weapons slipping from them in fear, overwhelmed by the mongooses, the enemies of the immortals fell.
Some mongooses entered the gaping mouths of the enemies and, pulling out their tongues like serpents' coils, bit them.
Other mongooses entered the ears of the gods' enemies; taking subtle forms, the brown ones entered various openings.
Seeing his own forces thus overwhelmed and wretched because of the mongooses, Karanka became enraged.
The other army commanders too, swift-handed and very mighty,
rained masses of arrows at the mongooses like clouds. The arrows shot from the mighty bows of the Daitya army commanders struck hard against the teeth of the mongooses.
From the diamond teeth of the mongooses, struck by hundreds of arrow-volleys from the commanders, fire burst forth. All five commanders together, in a single onslaught,
crushed the mongoose army with masses of arrows with gleaming heads. Their bodies torn by crores of arrows shot here and there by the commanders, the mongooses surrounded Nakuli.
Then that Nakuli, speech herself, sole mistress of all that is made of words, seeing the mongooses turn back, became greatly enraged.
She fixed on her Sharnga bow the great missile called Akshinanakula, facing every direction, its tip wreathed in flames of fire.
From that missile sprang crores of mongooses with diamond bodies, diamond hair and diamond fangs, exceedingly swift,
with the essence of diamond, dense, terrifying as a net of thunderbolts, swiftly tearing up the earth with diamond-like claws,
adorned with eyes gleaming like diamond jewels, like the fall of thunderbolts, snorting through their noses.
With crores of teeth they crushed the army of the gods' enemies; those sinless ones displayed many kinds of valour.
Thus by crores of mongooses, mighty and terrible as thunderbolts, the base Danavas were destroyed limb by limb and perished.
When the army was thus torn apart by troops of diamond mongooses,
and in that battle of a hundred akshauhinis only they themselves remained, the commanders, seized with great terror and rage, drew their bows and fought still harder.
Fighting with them in many ways, the queen of mongooses cut off Karanka's hard head with her pattisha.
Leaping again and again on Garuda, she cut off with her sword the heads of the four other enemies led by Kakavashita.
Seeing such swiftness in Nakuli, Shyamalamba
esteemed her highly as a great destroyer of wicked Asuras, and Shyamamba granted her the status of a deity of her own limbs.
Who does not feel delight on seeing extraordinary merit? The survivors of the slaughter, terrified, took refuge with Nakuli.
She, looking at them with compassion, smiled and said, "Do not fear. Go and tell your king the whole news of the battle."
Thus sent by her, they quickly looked over the battlefield and, glad yet afraid, fled back to Shunyaka.
Hearing that news, the fierce Bhanda became enraged.
Directed by him, he crushed the army of the Shaktis. Stationed at the shoulder of that best of Vetalas, the Danava then fought in many ways with the Shaktis.
Thus these seven wicked ones, like the seven oceans, arrogant, threw the army of the Shaktis there into confusion.
Those seven had formerly pleased the Sun by austerity, and the radiant one, pleased with their austerity, granted them a boon:
O illustrious sons of Kaikasi, I am fully pleased with your austerity; blessings on you — choose a boon.
When the lord of day had said this, the sons of Kaikasi, emaciated by austerity, earnestly asked for an unrestrained boon like this:

In battle may you be present in the hollows of our eyes, burning our opponents with your terrible radiance.
brahmandpuran:136:63	When you are present in our eyes, O Tapana, may everything within the range of our eyes become motionless, O lord.
brahmandpuran:136:64	The opposing soldiers looked upon by our eyes, kindled by your presence, will have their weapons paralysed.
brahmandpuran:136:65	Then, when their weapons are paralysed merely by our glance, O lord, the motionless enemies can easily be slain by us.
This boon was obtained long ago by the sons of Kaikasi from the Sun; by that boon they roamed the battle there, wild with pride.
Then, looked upon by their eyes possessed by the Sun, the Shaktis, their masses of weapons paralysed, lost their zeal in vain.
By those seven mighty sons of Kikasa the Shaktis' missiles and weapons were held fast, and they could make no effort.
Even when they made the effort, overpowered by the great paralysis of their weapons, the Shaktis sat silent, sighing.
Then, at daybreak, those Daityas, directed by their master and ready with various weapons, crushed the Shakti army.
Those Shaktis, inactive and without weapons, were shaken by their arrows, which pierced even diamond armour.
The Shaktis, their bodies pierced by floods of Daitya weapons and streaming with blood, shone in the battle like kankola creepers with fresh shoots.
Raising cries of woe, all the Shaktis, their weapons paralysed by them, cried out and took refuge with Lalita, the Queen.
Then, at the Goddess's command, the Dandanatha's bodyguard, the goddess Tiraskaranika, rose up on the battlefield.
Mounting the celestial car named Tamolipta, facing every direction, Mahamaya granted fearlessness to the Shaktis.
Dark as the tamala tree, wearing a dark bodice, on the dark-shadowed Tamolipta yoked with dark horses,
taking up the resounding bow named Vasanti Mohana, and roaring a lion's roar, she rained arrows like serpents.
The Daityas could not withstand the arrows issuing from the Mohana missile, like black serpents and like pestles turned downward.
Crushed here and there by the arrows of Mahamaya, the wicked ones led by Balahaka became supremely enraged.
Then Mother Tiraskarani, at the Dandanatha's command, released the great missile named Andha among the host of enemies.
Those seven led by Balahaka, arrogant with the Sun's boon, found their own eyes covered by the Andha missile.
By the Andha arrow shot from the great Mohana bow of the goddess Tiraskaranika, their eyes were blinded.
Blinded, those seven could see nothing; with the loss of their gaze, the paralysis of weapons ended.
Again, with lion-roars and weapons raised in hand, the Shaktis made ready for battle, eager to slay the Daityas.
Placing the mighty goddess Tiraskaranika in front, greatly pleased by her good stratagem, they fought.

Well done, well done, O illustrious Mother Tiraskaranika! Fittingly have you blinded these wicked enemies.
brahmandpuran:136:87	You are the great remedy for blinding the eyes of the wicked; by you this host of Daityas has had its sight bound.
brahmandpuran:136:88	O Goddess, this work of the gods has been well accomplished by you, since you have brought calamity on these who were invincible for us.
brahmandpuran:136:89	Hearing that these seven evil great Asuras have been slain by you alone, Lalita will attain supreme satisfaction.
brahmandpuran:136:90	When this is done by you, Dandini will be pleased, and the illustrious Mantrini too will surely attain the highest joy.
brahmandpuran:136:91	Therefore you yourself subdue these seven on the battlefield; we, with weapons raised, will destroy their entire army.
Thus urged by those Shaktis, eager for battle, she went on the Tamolipta car against the forces of Balahaka.
Seeing her coming, those seven base enemies of the gods quickly remembered once more the boon of the Sun.
But though the Sun's power entered their eyes, it could not stop her; being in the eye, it was overpowered by the splendour of Tiraskarani.
The goddess of concealment seized by the hair the great Asura Balahaka of mighty strength and valour, blinded by the boon, the missile and his rage, and cut him down with her sword.
Cutting off with an arrow the head of his vulture mount, Tiraskarani went toward Suchimukha.
Severing his hard head with the stroke of her pattisha, she slowly brought death to the other five as well.
Making a garland for her neck of the seven Daitya heads, tied together by their hair, the goddess of concealment roared.
The Shaktis, swooning with anger, slew that entire army and made many rivers flow with the waters of its blood.
There a great wonder was performed by Mother Mahamaya through her power of obstructing the sight of the generals led by Balahaka.
A few survivors, filled with great terror, in deep distress, went for refuge to the lord of Shunyaka, crying out.
They praised Dandini and Mahamaya again and again, and, receiving from her another grace in the form of sight, they rejoiced.
The Shaktis there, nodding their heads and saying "Well done, well done," praised the goddess Tiraskaranika at every step.
By the sharp arrows shot from the bow drawn by Kameshvari's hand, his armour pierced, Vishanga, deeply shaken, fled with the surviving warriors.
That wicked Danava was not slain by them, because he was to be slain only by the Dandanatha's arrow, radiant like the staff of death.
When that wicked Vishanga, Bhanda's brother, had fled, the night gave way to dawn and the directions grew clear.
